## Guest spotlight

**Ted Xiao** (Project Prometheus, previously Google DeepMind) told the last decade of robot learning as three eras, mostly through the work of the Google teams he was part of, and said so [▶ 03:11](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=191). The starting thesis, around 2016, was that robot hardware was nearly ready (a teleoperated robot could already tidy a room decades ago) and that the missing piece was intelligence, which deep learning was then supplying in games such as Atari and Go [▶ 02:34](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=154).

The first era, **existence proofs** (about 2016 to 2021), asked whether end-to-end learning on real robots could work at all. Google built "arm farms" of many robots collecting grasps around the clock [▶ 05:38](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=338), and QT-Opt applied Q-learning to continuous actions and camera images, trained on over half a million grasps [▶ 06:25](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=385). Online RL at that scale proved hard to run, so the team bet more on imitation (BC-Z) [▶ 08:14](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=494) and on learning from unstructured play data [▶ 09:03](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=543), and then started over with a fleet of robots collecting demonstrations of hundreds of tasks for a year and a half [▶ 09:56](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=596).

The second era, **foundation models**, borrowed the recipe this lecture describes: treat everything as tokens, reuse pre-trained models, and learn offline from large demonstration sets [▶ 12:19](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=739). RT-1 was a 35-million-parameter transformer from images and instructions to discretized action tokens, running at 3 Hz across hundreds of tasks [▶ 13:34](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=814). Language models were also used off the shelf: as planners whose suggestions were grounded by a value function saying which skills the robot could actually do now [▶ 15:59](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=959), and for relabeling robot data with richer instructions [▶ 17:08](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1028). RT-2 then made a VLM itself the policy, answering "what should the robot do?" with action tokens, and co-trained on web and robot data so web knowledge transferred to new objects [▶ 18:11](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1091). The Open X-Embodiment project pooled data from many labs and robots ("over 30 research labs", in his words) [▶ 19:35](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1175).

The third era, **scale**, is the present: large investments in turning those prototypes into products [▶ 22:01](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1321). His examples include Gemini Robotics, which combined a frontier multimodal model with dexterous data from the ALOHA platform (this week's discussion paper) [▶ 22:52](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1372) and, in its 1.5 version, one policy trained across several robot bodies with a shared action space [▶ 23:45](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1425); new evaluation methods, since real-world comparisons need thousands of trials [▶ 25:52](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1552); and many competing bets on data: wearable gloves, egocentric video, deployment data [▶ 26:04](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1564). He closed with open questions: the role of world models, the value of robot-free data, reasoning models, and how to unite manipulation, learned mostly by imitation, with locomotion, learned by RL in simulation [▶ 27:29](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1649). In the Q&A he expects high-quality teleoperation data to stay essential until training on cheaper, broader data is better understood [▶ 29:31](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1771), and he sees video-pretrained models as promising but doubts they replace text-based reasoning [▶ 32:41](https://youtu.be/VS7Ulaugevg?t=1961).

**How it connects to this week.** The talk is the lecture's thesis told as history: each era moved closer to "one transformer, tokens in and tokens out, trained on as much data as possible". RT-1 and RT-2 are the per-step action tokens of this page, and the move from them to FAST and to diffusion and flow heads ([Week 6](w06-generative-models.qmd)) is the move this week's last section explains. [Week 9](w09-generalist-robot-policies.qmd) takes up the generalist policies of the third era.

## Solved problems {#problems}

**1. Attention by hand.** Three tokens have values $v = (1, -1, 3)$, and the query's scores against their keys (already divided by $\sqrt{d}$) are $(2, 0, 1)$. Compute the attention weights and the output. Then apply a causal mask that hides the third token, and recompute.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^2 = 7.389$, $e^0 = 1$, $e^1 = 2.718$, summing to 11.107. Weights: 0.665, 0.090, 0.245. Output: $0.665 - 0.090 + 3 \times 0.245 = 1.31$. With the third score set to $-\infty$, its weight is 0 and the others renormalize: $7.389 / 8.389 = 0.881$ and $0.119$, so the output is $0.881 - 0.119 = 0.76$. Masking changes the answer because the hidden token carried the largest value.
:::

**2. Why order needs encoding.** Show that without positional information, permuting the input tokens permutes the attention outputs the same way, so a readout at the last position cannot depend on the order of the earlier tokens. What does this imply for the goal toy?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each output $\sum_j \alpha_{ij} v_j$ depends on the set of (key, value) pairs and on token $i$'s own query; the weights $\alpha_{ij}$ depend only on the contents $q_i \cdot k_j$. Reordering the other tokens reorders the terms of the sum without changing it. In the goal toy, the query is the last token, so its output is the same whichever goal came first: the head can only treat the two goals symmetrically. The symmetric answer with the least squared error is their average, and with independent standard normal goals its error is $\mathbb{E}[(g_2 - g_1)^2] / 4 = 2/4 = 0.5$, which is what training reached (`{python} f"{MSE[False].mean():.2f}"`).
:::

**3. Sizing a model.** You have a training budget of $10^{21}$ floating-point operations. Using $C \approx 6ND$ and $D \approx 20 N$, how many parameters and tokens are compute-optimal? If you instead train a model 4 times smaller with the same budget, how many tokens per parameter does it see?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Substituting, $C = 6 N \cdot 20 N = 120 N^2$, so $N = \sqrt{10^{21}/120} \approx 2.9 \times 10^9$ parameters and $D = 20 N \approx 5.8 \times 10^{10}$ tokens. A model of $N/4 \approx 7.2 \times 10^8$ parameters at the same compute sees $D = C/(6 \cdot N/4) = 4 \times 5.8 \times 10^{10} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{11}$ tokens: 320 tokens per parameter, 16 times the Chinchilla ratio. It is worse to train for this budget, but cheaper to run, which is the Llama 3 trade-off.
:::

**4. The token bill of per-step bins.** A VLA controls a 7-joint arm plus a gripper (8 action dimensions) at 50 Hz with one-second chunks, binned per dimension and per step. How many action tokens does one second of motion take? If the model decodes 200 tokens per second, can it keep up? What compression factor would let it plan each one-second chunk in a fifth of a second?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$8 \times 50 = 400$ tokens per second of motion. At 200 tokens per second the model needs 2 seconds to plan 1 second of motion: it falls behind. To plan in 0.2 s it may use 40 tokens, a compression factor of 10. In this page's toy, FAST compressed 50 Hz chunks by about `{python} f"{TOK[F_HI]['n_bins'] / TOK[F_HI]['n_fast']:.0f}"` times; real motions with more dimensions and sharper features would compress differently, so this is only an indication.
:::

**5. Ensemble weights.** With chunks of $k = 4$ and a temporal ensemble queried every step, how many predictions are averaged at step 10? With $m = 0.5$, what share of the weight does the oldest get, and what share the newest? After the goal moves, how many steps pass before every averaged prediction was made after the move?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Chunks from the queries at steps 7, 8, 9 and 10 cover step 10: four predictions. Weights $e^{-0.5 i}$ for $i = 0, \dots, 3$ are 1, 0.607, 0.368, 0.223, summing to 2.198; the oldest gets $1/2.198 = 45\%$, the newest $0.223/2.198 = 10\%$. After a move, the prediction made at the move's step enters at once, but the oldest made before the move leaves only $k - 1 = 3$ steps later, so from the fourth step on all four predictions know about the move. Weighting the oldest most, as larger $m$ does, slows the reaction further.
:::

## Recap

1. **Robots need sequences, in and out.** A single observation hides velocities and past events, and single-step decisions jitter. *Why it matters:* it is the reason the rest of the course uses history-conditioned, chunk-predicting policies.
2. **Attention gives direct access to the whole history.** Queries, keys and values implement a soft lookup; a causal mask makes it autoregressive; positional encodings supply order, and, as the goal toy shows, reach only as far as training required. *Why it matters:* this one mechanism underlies LLMs, VLMs and VLAs.
3. **Everything becomes tokens.** Sub-words by BPE, images by patches, vision and language aligned by contrastive training, early fusion, late fusion or native training. *Why it matters:* a robot policy built on a VLM inherits its tokenization and its knowledge.
4. **Scale is predictable.** Loss falls smoothly with model size, data and compute; Chinchilla's rule splits a budget at about 20 tokens per parameter. *Why it matters:* it frames the course's open question of what robot data at scale will buy.
5. **Per-step action bins break at high control rates.** Neighbouring tokens become almost entirely predictable from each other, and sequences become long; FAST compresses chunks with a DCT and BPE. *Why it matters:* high rates are what dexterous manipulation needs.
6. **Chunks trade reactivity for smoothness.** Open-loop chunks are smooth but blind and trust one estimate each; a temporal ensemble is smooth and as accurate as single-step control, but still reacts late. *Why it matters:* nearly every modern robot policy predicts action chunks.

## Cheat sheet & connections

| Name | Formula | Where |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Chain rule ★ | $p(x_{1:T}) = \prod_i p(x_i \mid x_{1:i-1})$ | @eq-chain |
| RNN | $h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)$ | @eq-rnn |
| Attention ★ | $\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})\,V$ | @eq-attention |
| Causal mask | $s_{ij} = -\infty$ for $j > i$ | @eq-causal |
| Positional encodings | $e_i + \mathrm{PE}(i)$; $s_{ij} + b(i - j)$ | @eq-position |
| RoPE | $(R_i q)^\top (R_j k) = q^\top R_{j-i} k$ | @eq-rope |
| Teacher forcing | $-\frac{1}{T}\sum_t \log p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$ | @eq-teacher |
| Chinchilla ★ | $C \approx 6ND$, $D^* \approx 20 N^*$ | @eq-scaling |
| CLIP | symmetric softmax over $s_{ij}/\tau$ | @eq-clip |
| Flamingo gate | $x + \tanh(\alpha)\,\text{CrossAttn}$ | @eq-flamingo |
| Action bins | quantile-normalize, 256 bins | @eq-bins |
| Chunk, ensemble | $\pi(a_{t:t+k} \mid o_t)$, $w_i = e^{-mi}$ | @eq-ensemble |
| DCT (FAST) | $c_j = \nu_j \sum_n u_n \cos(\cdot)$ | @eq-dct |

**Common pitfalls.**

- Forgetting the causal mask in training: the model sees each answer and learns to copy it, then fails at generation.
- Assuming relative positional encodings give long-range memory for free: they let the model run on longer inputs, not use what lies beyond the distances it learned.
- Min-max normalizing actions: one outlier wastes most of the bins.
- Judging an action tokenizer by next-token loss alone: at high rates a low loss can mean "copy the last token".
- Executing long chunks open loop in a changing world: the robot is blind until the next query.
- Comparing chunk sizes on smoothness only: accuracy and reaction time move the other way.

**Connections.** [Week 1](w01-introduction.qmd#tokens) introduced actions as tokens; this week explains the transformer that reads them and why the simplest tokenization fails at speed. [Week 3](w03-imitation-learning.qmd)'s behavior cloning is what ACT does with chunks, and chunking shortens the effective horizon over which Week 3's errors compound. [Weeks 4](w04-reinforcement-learning-1.qmd) and [5](w05-reinforcement-learning-2.qmd) maximize return, while the Decision Transformer conditions on it. [Week 6](w06-generative-models.qmd)'s diffusion and flow policies are the main alternative to autoregressive action tokens, and π0's flow head is the comparison point for FAST. [Week 9](w09-generalist-robot-policies.qmd) builds generalist VLAs from all of these pieces. In the ADM Companion: [beliefs]({{< var adm_url >}}/part4/ch19-beliefs.html#beliefs) and [the belief update]({{< var adm_url >}}/part4/ch19-beliefs.html#the-belief-update), the principled way to act on a history, and [controllers that remember]({{< var adm_url >}}/part4/ch23-controller-abstractions.html#a-policy-that-remembers-just-enough).
